prize_parts.citation: for foundational contributions to the theory of nominal rigidities and monetary policy rules that underpin the modern analysis of monetary policy

statement.case_for: B015 is the strongest case on the shortlist when the common criteria are applied: a specific scientific contribution, durable influence, and an explanatory framework that organises data. Calvo's tractable time-dependent pricing, Taylor's staggered contracts and policy rule, and Woodford's micro-founded synthesis together gave economics a framework that is both analytically usable and tied to measurement of how monetary policy works. Its influence on central-bank practice and on a large body of macroeconomic research has persisted through the post-2008 and post-2020 inflation episodes, and the framework has been revised rather than displaced. Ten of eleven members ranked it, seven of them in their top three, and I give that weight only as a signal that the attribution argument is not idiosyncratic. It is not evidence of merit. My own reasoning is the maturity of the evidence and the clarity of the three conceptual building blocks. I prefer a single-part prize because it keeps the citation focused, and a second part would force a split of credit across scholars with unclear boundaries.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. The ballot credits eight names, and Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets made contributions to estimation, the canonical New Keynesian model and medium-scale quantification that are arguably co-equal to those of the three names I propose. Calvo's and Taylor's key contributions are older than the synthesis, so a three-person prize risks under-crediting the empirical and quantitative phase. The framework's performance after 2021 and the heterogeneous-agent critique also leave real doubt about how settled its explanatory power is. Prior macroeconomics prizes on expectations and monetary policy may further reduce the marginal case.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B015 first, noting that a three-person prize naturally splits between staggered pricing and contracts (Calvo, Taylor) and the integrated framework (Woodford), and that omitting Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets is a real cost.
responses.response: I agree with the structure of the split and with calling the omission a real cost. I go further on one point: that cost is largest on the estimation side, where Christiano-Eichenbaum-Evans and Smets-Wouters turned the framework into something that fits the data. That part of the credit has no obvious home in a Calvo-Taylor-Woodford prize. Given the three-person limit, I think the citation should be worded around the theory of nominal rigidities and policy rules, not around empirical validation. I also read Hassler's point about post-2021 inflation as a qualification that should be reflected in the citation's wording.

responses.point: Stromberg ranks B050 first with Kiyotaki and Moore. His argument is that collateral constraints turn small shocks into persistent amplified credit cycles, and that a two-name award is the cleanest attribution because the accelerator line is partly covered by the 2022 prize. He also concedes that direct empirical identification of the original mechanism is mixed.
responses.response: I accept that B050 has the cleaner attribution: two names against a diffuse eight. That is a real advantage over B015 and I weigh it. Where I differ is on how much weight the difference deserves. A clear attribution to a theory-led mechanism whose empirical identification Stromberg himself calls mixed is a weaker basis than a framework that has been used and tested in policy for decades. My own view of Goldin's case is that a framework paired with data discovery is the stronger kind of contribution. B050 is therefore not in my alternatives, but I would revisit that if the discussion shows the post-crisis empirical record is stronger than the opening statements suggest.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B038 first, arguing that firm heterogeneity and selection turned trade theory into a framework that fits firm-level microdata, with strong empirical discipline and a natural succession from the 2008 new trade theory prize. He also flags that quantitative gains-from-trade results depend on elasticity assumptions.
responses.response: I find the B038 case close to B015 in strength, which is why it is my first alternative. The tight link between theory and microdata is the quality I value most. I qualify it on attribution: Boppart himself notes the credit split with Helpman's other work, and I would add that Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are outside the credited names and hold a serious claim on the empirical firm-level facts. That leaves the Melitz-Helpman pairing less clean than it looks. The model-dependent welfare magnitudes he mentions are comparable in kind to the framework-dependence concerns I have about B015, so I do not think this separates the two cases.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranks B036 first, arguing that it combines a conceptual task framework with credible local-labour-market identification, and that Acemoglu's task-model work and the generalisability of the trade-shock estimates are the main attribution and robustness issues.
responses.response: I share his view that the combination of new data, an explanatory framework and credible identification is what makes B036 compelling, which is why it is an alternative for me. I would qualify it in two ways. The candidate bundles two strands with different authorship, so any three-name set splits credit between the task and skill-premium evidence and the China-shock work. Dorn is also left out despite co-authoring the key papers. The Acemoglu overlap he flags is a further reason I hold B036 below B015, where the attribution problem is dispersion within one framework rather than a bundle of two.

uncertainties: Whether a different three-name split within B015, for example including Gali or Gertler, would be more defensible than Calvo, Taylor and Woodford, and how much weight the committee gives the estimation phase against the originating theory.
How the post-2021 inflation episode and the heterogeneous-agent critique should affect the assessment of the framework's maturity and explanatory standing.
Whether B038 or B036 deserves priority on the strength of microdata-based evidence, given the attribution problems each carries.
My assessments rely on general knowledge of the literature, not on independently verified citation or credit records.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile: no frequent co-author or institutional tie to any credited name on the shortlist is listed. My research field (labour economics and crime) is adjacent to B036, and I treat that as a field proximity rather than a personal connection.
